reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: configuration allocates seller liability, it is fixed early regardless of fund custody, and it drives four linked outcomes
Opening case: a customer's partial refund after the studio was paid raises whose balance pays it
How this part differs from earlier parts: a platform intermediary splits liability via its account setup, unlike merchant of record
Thesis stated: liability follows the configured account model, fixed upfront, with Stripe and Adyen evidence
The loss assignment also governs verification, post-payout refunds and embedded finance / Larkfield's roughly €156M exposure figure
Limits of the evidence from provider documentation
Roadmap of the four chapters in the order a platform encounters them
Chapter preview: identifying the merchant and loss bearer, with Larkfield teams disagreeing
Chapter preview: ongoing seller verification and payout suspension, illustrated by a stalled climbing gym
Chapter preview: splitting payments and paying out provisionally, with Larkfield's ledger gap from post-payout refunds
Chapter preview: licensed backing and constraints for seller accounts, cards and lending, ending in a deferred card
Reading guidance: enter anywhere but the first chapter underpins the rest; start there

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Every outline summary agrees with the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph (p01-p11); the KEY POINTS callout is house format and matches no spec paragraph.

results.quote: Larkfield's figure for what that decision exposes it to is about €156 million: the online card volume that, at any time, has been paid out and can still be disputed.
results.finding: The outliner read ¶4 as two ideas (the assignment settles three more things / Larkfield's €156M exposure). The spec makes the €156M figure evidence for p04's idea (the figure a team keeps once it decides the loss bearer first), but the draft appends it with no link to that idea, so it reads as a second topic.
Each unit traces to the thesis: p01-p06 pose the question, state the claim and its limits and give the order; p07-p10 each introduce the chapter carrying P7-1..P7-4; p11 routes the reader.

Figure 1 and Figure 2 are introduced by the surrounding prose and their captions state what they show; the Stripe quotation and the Adyen paraphrase are explained as where each provider records the assignment; the €156M figure is defined. (The unexplained two-second authorization fact is recorded under known_before_new.)

All transitions_in read at their boundaries express the declared relationship and carry over/introduce as declared: p02 contrast ('Parts I to VI never had to ask that question'), p03 ('That division is the part's claim'), p04 additional support ('The same assignment settles three more things'), p05 limits ('the comparison stops in named places'), p06 sequence, chapters section elaboration (end of p06), p08 cause_effect ('follows from every seller being an account'), p09 sequence ('takes the verified seller's first payment'), p10 elaboration ('starts from the seller balance ...'), conclusion summary.

Both flow readers describe the declared large_to_small order (case -> claim -> what it decides -> chapters) and the prerequisite order of chapters, and mark no section's position unclear. Material lost-thread points are recorded as separate results.

results.quote: Larkfield's figure for what that decision exposes it to is about €156 million: the online card volume that, at any time, has been paid out and can still be disputed.
results.finding: Both readers lost the thread here: a large new number arrives with no bridge from Mila's €84.00 or from the 'one decision' sentence, its definition needs a second reading, and nothing later uses it. The spec's placement in p04 is defensible; the prose needs to tie the figure to the claim (how much rides on the assignment, scaled up from Mila's refund).

results.quote: Neither company publishes a completion rate for seller sign-up. Accounts for a platform's sellers were in preview at Stripe and in development at Adyen in November 2026, on documentation pages that carry no date.
results.finding: Both readers found the evidence-limits paragraph out of place: it states limits for chapters (sign-up, seller accounts) the reader has not yet been introduced to and interrupts the move from claim and Figure 2 to the chapter list; both proposed moving it after the chapter list. The difficulty comes from the order the spec declares and defends in flow.rationale (p05 before the list), so it is a decision for the author.

results.quote: [[part-6]] ended on the one arrangement that moves the seller's role, the merchant of record, in which a provider sells in its own name
results.finding: Both readers had to re-read this sentence: 'moves the seller's role' is hard to parse, the appositive 'the merchant of record' is ambiguous, and 'the opposite arrangement' suggests a mirror image that the next sentence does not quite give. The spec's contrast is sound; the wording obscures it.

results.quote: Larkfield's proposed card for Tuesday's sales ends as a reasoned "not yet".
results.finding: Both readers could not tell what 'a card for Tuesday's sales' is (spending not-yet-paid-out sales? an advance?); the other three chapter paragraphs end on a clear case, this one is cryptic. The spec describes it as an instant-payout card for studios.

results.quote: Sources are cited in each chapter; this introduction makes no factual claim of its own.
results.finding: Both readers stopped because the sentence contradicts the body, which quotes Stripe's documentation, paraphrases Adyen's and states dated preview and pilot status. The spec's non-goal means the page makes no claim a chapter does not make and cite; the sentence should say that. (Content, not position, of the house-format section.)

results.quote: A reader with one platform decision in hand can enter at its chapter; the later three all reuse the loss assignment that the first one explains. By the end of the part you can say which balance funds Mila's €84.00 on each provider, and why. The first chapter answers her question in general form. Begin with [[platform-payment-models]].
results.finding: Both readers found the section pulling two ways: enter at any chapter, then 'Begin with' the first for everyone. The spec's so_what is conditional (a reader with a decision enters at its chapter; one without the first chapter's three answers starts there); the draft drops the condition.

results.quote: Stripe documents the provider as a standing option for the loss bearer.
results.finding: Reader A could not tell whether 'standing option' means always available or default, set beside 'Adyen's default is the platform'. Only one reader.

results.quote: The merchant is whoever the customer understands they are buying from, and the configuration has to agree with that; it then books the payment and assigns the loss.
results.finding: Reader A: 'it' is ambiguous between the merchant and the configuration. Only one reader.

results.quote: Adyen's standard deadline is 30 days for payout capabilities and 60 for receiving payments.
results.finding: Reader A: deadline for what, counted from when, is not said. Only one reader.

results.quote: Who stands behind a seller also decides who collects verification data, where a refund after payout is booked, and whether accounts and cards may be offered.
results.finding: Reader B: the bullet says four and lists three; the fourth (the loss assignment itself) is left implicit in the stand-alone block. Only one reader.

results.quote: The assignment is made when accounts and payments are configured, long before the first loss.
results.finding: Reader B: the bold lead's 'it' has no antecedent inside the bullet, and lead and sentence make different points. Only one reader.

The spec's does_not_know terms are glossed or only named as allowed: liable balance account (glossed in ¶3), account model (glossed in ¶2), split (glossed in Chapters ¶3), exposure (€156M defined), charge type and capability named. Failures below are terms outside the spec's lists.

results.quote: Ironworks Climbing, one of Larkfield's 230 Frozen Studios, went nine days in May 2026
results.finding: 'Frozen Studios' is capitalised as a defined term but never defined; both flow readers had to infer it means studios whose payouts were frozen.

results.quote: Accounts for a platform's sellers were in preview at Stripe and in development at Adyen in November 2026
results.finding: 'Accounts' here means bank-style accounts offered to sellers (embedded finance), while everywhere before it means the seller's account at the provider (the account model). Both flow readers misread it; one first took it to mean the account model itself was in preview.

results.quote: Both providers give the platform's server two seconds to answer a card authorization
results.finding: Nothing on the page says that a platform issuing cards takes part in card authorization, so the two-second limit arrives without the concept that makes it matter. Both flow readers reported it as unexplained.
Opens on a puzzling scenario with exact amounts and dates, bridges from Parts I-VI, states the claim and gives the roadmap; no weak pattern.
The conclusion routes the reader and calls back to the hook; it is not a restatement-only or new-material ending.

It synthesises (the later three chapters reuse the first chapter's loss assignment; by the end the reader can say which balance funds Mila's refund) and answers so-what with where to start. The dropped condition on 'Begin with' is recorded under flow_is_followable.
Calls back to Mila's €84.00 and promises the reader can say which balance funds it on each provider, as the spec's callback requires.

The intro-only reader predicted the four chapters in the right order and subjects (merchant and loss; verification; split, payout and reversal; accounts, cards and financing), matching the roadmap promise kept in 'chapters'.

Cold reader stated the claim (the account model assigns sellers' losses at configuration, not undone by not holding funds) and the four chapters in order, including refunds after the studio had been paid; matches expected.

Rubric: the body opens on Mila's €84.00 request of 18 March 2027 for seven unused classes on a €120.00 pass, Studio Noord paid €117.47 on Thursday 11 March, and says 'The open question is whose balance it comes out of today' without answering it; 'Where to Begin' defers the answer to the part.
